Title: What business problem should getBill solve, and how will you know it is solved?
Why it matters: The goal decides every other answer and how success is measured.
Examples of possible answers: Finance gets monthly cost reports without manual work. Each customer receives an accurate statement within three business days. Costs are charged back to departments.

Title: Whose AWS costs are these: FPT's own accounts, FPT's customers' accounts, or both?
Why it matters: Billing your own usage and rebilling customers have different rules, recipients and confidentiality.
Examples of possible answers: FPT's internal accounts only. Customer accounts that FPT resells or manages. Both, kept separate.

Title: Who will use getBill, and how technical are they?
Why it matters: It decides the kind of interface and how much must be automatic.
Examples of possible answers: Cloud engineers. Finance analysts. Account managers. Customers themselves.

Title: How should people use it?
Why it matters: A command line, a web page and a fully automatic service are very different products.
Examples of possible answers: A command line. A web page. A request by email or chat. Fully automatic with no person involved.

Title: What should the result look like for each audience?
Why it matters: The output format decides the processing and the delivery.
Examples of possible answers: Excel workbooks. CSV files. PDF statements. A dashboard such as Amazon QuickSight. Rows in a data warehouse. An API.

Title: Which languages and number formats must the output use?
Why it matters: Recipients may expect their local language and formats.
Examples of possible answers: English. Vietnamese. Both. Decimal comma or decimal point.

Title: Which currency must the results show, and where do exchange rates come from?
Why it matters: AWS bills in US dollars, but recipients may need another currency.
Examples of possible answers: US dollars only. Vietnamese dong at the bank's month-end rate. Both side by side.

Title: Is there a deadline or a first milestone?
Why it matters: It decides what to build first.
Examples of possible answers: A first customer report by a given date. Internal use first, customers later.

Title: Which team or person owns the billing data, and who is the contact when a file is late or wrong?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: Someone must fix a broken or missing file.
Examples of possible answers: The cloud operations team. The finance team. An AWS partner or reseller portal.

Title: What produces the billing files?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: Each source has its own columns, names and layout.
Examples of possible answers: AWS Data Exports (CUR 2.0). The older AWS Cost and Usage Report. AWS Data Exports in the FOCUS format. A reseller or partner billing portal. Another internal system.

Title: Which AWS accounts do the files cover, and in which account is the export created?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: An export in the management (payer) account covers every account. One in a member account covers only that account.
Examples of possible answers: One management account for the whole organization. Several organizations. Each customer's own account.

Title: Are there several sources that must be combined, such as several AWS organizations or other clouds?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: Combining sources needs matching rules.
Examples of possible answers: One AWS organization. Several organizations. AWS plus Azure or Google Cloud.

Title: Which columns, filters and details does the export include?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: Columns and details decide file size and what recipients can see.
Examples of possible answers: All columns. Selected columns only. Resource IDs included or not. Split cost allocation data for containers.

Title: What time detail does the export have?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: Hourly data is many times larger than daily or monthly data.
Examples of possible answers: Hourly. Daily. Monthly.

Title: In which file formats and compression do the files arrive, now and in the future?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: The pipeline must read every format that arrives.
Examples of possible answers: Parquet with Snappy, gzip or Zstandard compression. CSV compressed with gzip. ZIP archives. Plain CSV. Excel. JSON.

Title: Where exactly are the files stored, and how are they organized?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: The pipeline must find the right files for each month.
Examples of possible answers: An S3 bucket with one folder for each month, such as BILLING_PERIOD=2026-10. Several part files for each month. A manifest file that lists the parts. A shared drive. An email attachment.

Title: Should all parts of a month be treated as one data set?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: Recipients usually expect one result for each month.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, always join the parts. No, keep each part separate.

Title: How often do new or updated files arrive?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: It decides when processing runs.
Examples of possible answers: Several times a day. Once a day. Once a month after the month closes.

Title: Can a closed month change later, and what should happen then?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: AWS can restate a month after credits or refunds. Recipients need final numbers and need to know when numbers change.
Examples of possible answers: Ignore changes after the deadline. Reprocess and send a corrected version. Send only the differences.

Title: How large is a typical file, and how large is the largest you expect?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: Size decides speed, cost and which output formats can hold the data.
Examples of possible answers: A few megabytes. Hundreds of megabytes. Several gigabytes each month.

Title: In which AWS Regions are the files stored?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: Moving data across Regions costs more and may be restricted.
Examples of possible answers: One Region. Several Regions. Data must stay in a given country.

Title: Who may write the files, and who may read them?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: Each writer and reader needs its own permissions.
Examples of possible answers: Only AWS Data Exports writes. Only the getBill service reads. Engineers may also read.

Title: How are the source files encrypted, and who controls the keys?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: A customer-managed key needs permission for every reader.
Examples of possible answers: S3-managed keys. An AWS KMS key owned by the security team.

Title: How long are source files kept, and can earlier versions be recovered?
Section: 1. Source: where the billing files come from
Why it matters: An overwritten file can be lost for good.
Examples of possible answers: Kept forever. Kept for 13 months. S3 versioning turned on.

Title: Who receives the results?
Why it matters: The recipients decide the content, the format and who may see what.
Examples of possible answers: The finance team. Budget owners for each department. Each customer. Auditors.

Title: How should each recipient receive the results?
Why it matters: Many recipients cannot use cloud storage directly.
Examples of possible answers: An email attachment. A link that expires. A shared drive such as SharePoint or Google Drive. An S3 bucket in their own AWS account. A web portal.

Title: Should each recipient see only part of the data?
Why it matters: Sending all lines to everyone can expose other customers' or departments' costs.
Examples of possible answers: Only their own AWS accounts. Only their cost center or tag. Everything.

Title: How should results be named and organized?
Why it matters: Clear names stop people from opening the wrong month or customer.
Examples of possible answers: By month. By month and customer. By month, customer and version number.

Title: Who may read and who may change the delivered results?
Why it matters: Billing results are confidential.
Examples of possible answers: Only the recipient. The recipient and finance. Read-only for everyone.

Title: Should recipients be told when results are ready, and how?
Why it matters: Without a notice, people use old results or keep checking.
Examples of possible answers: An email. A chat message in Teams or Slack. No notice.

Title: What should happen when results for the same month already exist?
Why it matters: Recipients need to know which version is current.
Examples of possible answers: Replace them. Keep both with a version number. Keep both and mark the old one as replaced.

Title: May results be delivered into another organization's AWS account, and under what rules?
Why it matters: Cross-organization delivery needs agreements and permissions.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, into each customer's own account. No, only into FPT's accounts.

Title: What content should each audience receive?
Why it matters: Raw lines, summaries and statements are different products.
Examples of possible answers: Every line item. Totals by account, service, Region or tag. Pivot tables. Charts. An invoice-style statement.

Title: Which cost measure should recipients see?
Why it matters: Each measure gives a different total.
Examples of possible answers: Unblended cost. Net cost after discounts. Amortized cost for Savings Plans and Reserved Instances. Public list price.

Title: Should prices be changed before recipients see them?
Why it matters: Resellers often add a margin, apply a discount, or remove AWS credits.
Examples of possible answers: No changes. Add a markup percentage. Apply a customer-specific discount. Hide credits.

Title: Which columns should recipients see, with what names and in what order?
Why it matters: Raw technical column names are hard for finance users.
Examples of possible answers: All original columns. A short list with plain names. Different columns for each audience.

Title: How should values be shown?
Why it matters: Wrong types break totals and change account IDs.
Examples of possible answers: Costs as numbers with two decimal places. Account IDs as text. Dates in a set format.

Title: Which time zone should dates and times use?
Why it matters: Daily totals change with the time zone.
Examples of possible answers: UTC. Vietnam time. Each recipient's own time zone.

Title: How should tax, credits, refunds and support fees be treated?
Why it matters: They change the totals recipients see.
Examples of possible answers: Show them as separate lines. Include them in the totals. Leave them out.

Title: Where and how should processing run?
Why it matters: It decides reliability, cost and who must be available.
Examples of possible answers: On a person's computer when needed. A scheduled job in AWS. Automatically each time a new file arrives.

Title: What should happen when a month is too large for the chosen output format?
Why it matters: Excel, email and some tools have size limits.
Examples of possible answers: Split it into several sheets or files. Summarize it. Use a different format for large months.

Title: What should happen when one file or one recipient fails?
Why it matters: One failure should not block everyone else.
Examples of possible answers: Continue with the others and report the failure. Stop everything until it is fixed.

Title: Must processing be safe to run again for the same month?
Why it matters: Re-runs happen after failures and restatements.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, a re-run must give the same results without duplicates.

Title: May billing data be copied to a person's computer during processing?
Why it matters: Copies on laptops can leak.
Examples of possible answers: Yes. Only to company-managed computers. No, it must stay in AWS.

Title: After processing, who must receive what, besides the recipients in section 2?
Why it matters: The data owner or finance may need a copy or a confirmation.
Examples of possible answers: A copy to finance. A confirmation to the data owner. Nothing more.

Title: Does anyone need a receipt for each run?
Why it matters: A receipt shows that nothing was lost.
Examples of possible answers: A list of files, row counts and totals. A signed summary. No receipt.

Title: Who must be told about failures, and how quickly?
Why it matters: A failure nobody sees means missing reports.
Examples of possible answers: The operations team within an hour. The product owner by the next morning.

Title: Do recipients send anything back, such as approvals, disputes or corrections?
Why it matters: Some processes need a sign-off for each month.
Examples of possible answers: Approval by email. Disputes through a ticket system. Nothing.

Title: How long must source files and results be kept, and why?
Why it matters: Audit, tax and contract rules can set minimum periods.
Examples of possible answers: Ten years for tax records. Seven years under a contract. Thirteen months.

Title: Where should archives be kept?
Why it matters: Old files cost less in cheaper storage.
Examples of possible answers: S3 Glacier after 90 days. A separate archive account. A records system.

Title: Must archives be impossible to change or delete?
Why it matters: Auditors may need proof that records were not altered.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, with S3 Object Lock. No.

Title: When must files be deleted, and who approves it?
Why it matters: Keeping data too long can also break policy or contracts.
Examples of possible answers: Automatically after the retention period. Only with the data owner's approval.

Title: Should every version of a month's results be kept, or only the latest?
Why it matters: Earlier versions show what recipients saw on each date.
Examples of possible answers: Every version. Only the final version.

Title: How must people and automated jobs sign in to AWS?
Why it matters: Shared keys are hard to control and to revoke.
Examples of possible answers: IAM Identity Center (SSO) for people. IAM roles for automated jobs. No long-term access keys.

Title: How sensitive is this data, and how is it classified?
Why it matters: Account names, tags and resource IDs can reveal customers, projects or people.
Examples of possible answers: Confidential. Internal. Contains personal data.

Title: Which rules apply, such as contracts, data protection laws or internal policies?
Why it matters: Rules can limit where data goes and who may see it.
Examples of possible answers: Customer contracts. Vietnam's personal data protection rules. Company security policy.

Title: Must there be an audit record of who ran what, when, on which files?
Why it matters: Audits and incident reviews need it.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, kept for one year. Yes, through AWS CloudTrail. No.

Title: How must data be encrypted in transit and at rest?
Why it matters: Billing data is confidential.
Examples of possible answers: AWS defaults. A company-managed key for everything.

Title: Who must approve sharing billing data outside the company?
Why it matters: Sending customer costs to the wrong place is a serious incident.
Examples of possible answers: The data owner. Legal. Security.

Title: How should the results be checked against the source?
Why it matters: A mismatch means lost or changed data.
Examples of possible answers: Totals must match exactly. Totals must match to the cent. Row counts must match.

Title: Must the results match the AWS invoice for each month?
Why it matters: Finance reconciles against the invoice.
Examples of possible answers: Yes, exactly. Yes, within a stated tolerance. No.

Title: When is a month final?
Why it matters: Reporting before AWS closes a month gives numbers that change later.
Examples of possible answers: When AWS issues the invoice. A fixed number of days after the month ends.

Title: What should happen when the source file's columns or layout change?
Why it matters: A changed export can silently break reports.
Examples of possible answers: Stop and alert. Continue and warn. Adapt automatically.

Title: Who signs off that the results are correct before they are sent?
Why it matters: Errors in customer statements are costly.
Examples of possible answers: Finance reviews each month. Automatic checks are enough.

Title: Who owns and supports getBill, and who is the backup?
Why it matters: Someone must fix it when it fails, even during holidays.
Examples of possible answers: The cloud team, with a named backup. The finance systems team.

Title: By what date or time must results be ready each month?
Why it matters: A deadline decides the schedule and the alerts.
Examples of possible answers: By the third business day. Within one day of each new file.

Title: What budget is there to run it?
Why it matters: Storage, processing and data transfer cost money every month.
Examples of possible answers: A fixed monthly limit. Charged back to each recipient.

Title: How many accounts, customers, files and recipients must it handle now, and in two years?
Why it matters: Growth can pass limits that are safe today.
Examples of possible answers: Ten accounts and one recipient now. Hundreds of customers later.

Title: How should changes to getBill be approved, tested and released?
Why it matters: Untested changes can corrupt reports.
Examples of possible answers: Automatic tests and a review for every change. A test month before each release.

Title: What must be tested with real data before getBill is trusted?
Why it matters: A test with real data shows real sizes, formats and permissions.
Examples of possible answers: One full month for one account. A parallel run beside the current process.

Title: Is there a current manual process that getBill replaces, and when can it stop?
Why it matters: A safe switch-over needs both to run for a while.
Examples of possible answers: An analyst exports Excel files by hand each month. Nothing exists yet.

Title: What is the most rows one month can have?
Why it matters: Excel holds at most 1,048,576 rows in one sheet, and other formats have their own limits.
Examples of possible answers: Under one million. Several million. Not known yet.

Title: What is the most columns a file can have?
Why it matters: Some exports add one column for each tag key and grow very wide. Excel holds at most 16,384 columns.
Examples of possible answers: Under 150. Several hundred. Not known yet.

Title: How many decimal places must costs keep, and may they be rounded?
Why it matters: Excel keeps only 15 significant digits, so very precise large numbers lose digits.
Examples of possible answers: Keep all decimal places. Round to two places for reports. Round only in summaries.

Title: What is the range of values, from the largest credit to the largest single cost?
Why it matters: A range check catches broken data.
Examples of possible answers: Credits down to minus 100,000 dollars. Single lines up to one million dollars.

Title: What range of dates must be handled, and how precise must times be?
Why it matters: Some tools only store dates in a set range or to the millisecond.
Examples of possible answers: The last ten years. Times to the second.

Title: What is the longest text in one field, such as a list of tags?
Why it matters: Excel holds at most 32,767 characters in one cell.
Examples of possible answers: Short tag lists. Hundreds of tags on some resources.

Title: What is the largest result a recipient can receive and open?
Why it matters: Email systems often refuse attachments over about 20 to 25 MB, and very large workbooks open slowly.
Examples of possible answers: Under 10 MB by email. Any size through a link.

Title: How many files can one month or one run contain, and how long may a run take?
Why it matters: Scheduled jobs often have time limits.
Examples of possible answers: Up to 100 files. A run must finish within one hour.

Title: How long can names be, such as customer names, file names and folder paths?
Why it matters: Some systems limit name lengths, such as Excel sheet names at 31 characters.
Examples of possible answers: Short codes. Full customer names.

Title: What is the largest number of accounts, tag keys and recipients in one month?
Why it matters: Large numbers change how results are split and delivered.
Examples of possible answers: Fifty accounts and twenty tag keys. Thousands of accounts.

Title: Month-end close. A month ends and AWS finalizes its costs. What should happen, and by when?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Everyday use
Why it matters: This is usually the main reason a billing pipeline exists.
Examples of possible answers: Monthly reports for every recipient by the third business day. One summary for finance, then statements for customers.

Title: Costs so far this month. Someone wants to see the current month's costs before it ends. Should getBill support that, and how often?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Everyday use
Why it matters: Month-to-date reports help people act before the month closes, but the numbers still change.
Examples of possible answers: A daily update marked "not final". A weekly update. Only final months.

Title: Customer statements. Each customer receives a statement of their AWS costs. What must a statement contain?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Everyday use
Why it matters: Statements often become invoices, so errors cost money and trust.
Examples of possible answers: Totals by service and account. Every line item. FPT's logo and terms. A statement number.

Title: Chargeback or showback inside the company. Costs are assigned to departments, projects or cost centers. How are they assigned?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Everyday use
Why it matters: Assigning costs needs clear rules for tags, accounts and shared costs.
Examples of possible answers: By the CostCenter tag. By AWS account. By AWS Cost Categories. Untagged costs go to a shared pool.

Title: Budget tracking. Someone compares spending with a budget. Should getBill show budgets, and warn when one is exceeded?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Everyday use
Why it matters: Budget warnings need the budget figures and a rule for when to warn.
Examples of possible answers: Show spending against each department's budget. Warn at 80% and at 100%. Not needed, because AWS Budgets is used.

Title: A sudden jump in cost. Costs rise unexpectedly, for example after a mistake. Should getBill point it out?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Everyday use
Why it matters: Catching a spike early can save a great deal of money.
Examples of possible answers: Highlight any service that costs 50% more than last month. Not needed, because AWS Cost Anomaly Detection is used.

Title: Forecast. Someone wants to know what the month or the year will cost. Should getBill estimate it?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Everyday use
Why it matters: A forecast needs history and a chosen method.
Examples of possible answers: An end-of-month estimate from the daily average. Not needed.

Title: One-off request. Someone asks for a specific extract, such as one account's database costs for last quarter. How should such requests be handled?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Everyday use
Why it matters: One-off requests are common and often urgent.
Examples of possible answers: Anyone can run a filtered report themselves. Requests go to the cloud team. Not supported.

Title: Audit request. An auditor asks for the billing records of a past period. What must be produced, and how fast?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Everyday use
Why it matters: Audits need complete, unchanged records and proof of where they came from.
Examples of possible answers: The original files and the results for any month in the last ten years, within five business days.

Title: A new customer or account starts mid-month. What should their first report or statement cover?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Changes to customers and accounts
Why it matters: Partial months need a clear start date.
Examples of possible answers: Costs from the day the account was linked. The whole month. Nothing until the next full month.

Title: A customer or account leaves mid-month. What should happen to their final report and to their stored data?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Changes to customers and accounts
Why it matters: Leaving customers need a final statement, and their data may have to be deleted.
Examples of possible answers: A final statement up to the leaving date. Data deleted after 90 days. Data kept for the retention period.

Title: An account moves between customers, departments or AWS organizations. Whose report should its costs appear in?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Changes to customers and accounts
Why it matters: A move splits one account's costs between two owners.
Examples of possible answers: Split by the date of the move. The new owner gets the whole month.

Title: Past months are needed. On the first run, or after a correction, earlier months must be processed. How far back?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Changes to customers and accounts
Why it matters: Back-filling needs the old files to still exist, and can take a long time.
Examples of possible answers: The last 12 months on the first run. Any month on request. Only months from now on.

Title: Savings Plans and Reserved Instances. Upfront or monthly commitment fees appear on one account but benefit many. How should they be shown?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Changes to customers and accounts
Why it matters: The choice changes every recipient's totals.
Examples of possible answers: Spread each fee over the accounts that used it. Show the fee where it was bought. Leave it out.

Title: Credits and refunds. AWS credits, promotional credits and refunds arrive. Who gets the benefit?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Changes to customers and accounts
Why it matters: Credits can be large, and passing them on is a business decision.
Examples of possible answers: Pass credits to the customer whose usage earned them. Keep credits for FPT. Show them on a separate line.

Title: Shared costs. Some costs serve everyone, such as the AWS Support plan, shared networks or tax. How should they be divided?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Changes to customers and accounts
Why it matters: Every shared cost needs a sharing rule, or totals will not add up.
Examples of possible answers: Divide in proportion to each recipient's spending. Charge them to a central budget. Show them separately.

Title: Prices or margins change mid-month. A reseller margin or a customer discount changes partway through a month. Which applies to which days?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: Changes to customers and accounts
Why it matters: Mixed rates in one month need a clear rule.
Examples of possible answers: The new rate from the day it changes. The new rate from the next month.

Title: The billing file is late or missing at the deadline. What should happen, and who should be told?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: When things go wrong
Why it matters: Recipients wait on the results, and someone must chase the source.
Examples of possible answers: Alert the data owner and wait. Send last month's figures marked as late. Tell the recipients about the delay.

Title: A file is incomplete, damaged or duplicated. What should getBill do?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: When things go wrong
Why it matters: Processing bad data produces wrong results.
Examples of possible answers: Stop and alert. Skip the bad file and continue. Remove duplicate lines automatically.

Title: AWS changes a month after it was delivered. See S11. Should the recipients get a corrected version, and how are they told?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: When things go wrong
Why it matters: A corrected statement can change money already invoiced.
Examples of possible answers: Send a corrected version with the changes marked. Adjust next month's statement instead.

Title: Wrong results were already sent. How are they withdrawn and replaced?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: When things go wrong
Why it matters: A wrong statement can reach a customer or an auditor.
Examples of possible answers: Recall the link and send a corrected version with an explanation. Send a correction notice only.

Title: A recipient's contact or access changes. For example, someone leaves the company. How is the list of recipients kept up to date?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: When things go wrong
Why it matters: Results sent to a former employee or a wrong address are a data leak.
Examples of possible answers: The account manager updates the list. The list comes from the company's directory.

Title: AWS changes the export's columns or format. See Q4. Who decides how getBill adapts?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: When things go wrong
Why it matters: AWS adds and renames columns from time to time.
Examples of possible answers: The cloud team updates getBill within a week. Reports pause until it is fixed.

Title: Data is lost or a service is down. For example, the source bucket is deleted, or an AWS Region is unavailable on the deadline. How quickly must getBill recover?
Section: 10. Scenarios and use cases: When things go wrong
Why it matters: Recovery needs copies of the data and a plan made in advance.
Examples of possible answers: Recover within one business day from a copy in another Region. Wait for AWS to recover.
